## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

The *Saṁghabhedakakkhandhaka* ("The chapter on schism in the Sangha", Kd 17) is the seventeenth chapter of the Khandhaka section in the Vinaya Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. It opens with the narrative of the going forth of several Sakyan relatives of the Buddha, prominent among whom are Anuruddha and Devadatta [SuttaCentral]. The narrative charts Devadatta's mounting ambition to assume control over the Sangha, incorporating the account of King Ajātasattu murdering his father and Devadatta's repeated attempts to assassinate the Buddha, culminating in an outright monastic schism (*saṅghabheda*) [SuttaCentral]. In response to Devadatta's maneuvers, the Buddha institutes the formal "announcement procedure" (*pakāsanīyakamma*), providing the Sangha with a communal mechanism to repudiate and distance itself from the deeds of a specific individual [SuttaCentral]. The treatise concludes with a detailed technical exposition defining the parameters, types, and implications of schism within the monastic order [SuttaCentral].
Full canonical parallels survive across multiple early Buddhist monastic recensions, including the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Saṅghabhedavastu* (preserved in Sanskrit, Tibetan, and Chinese), as well as the Saṅghabheda chapters of the Sarvāstivāda (Kd 16), Dharmaguptaka (Kd 15), and Mahīśāsaka (Kd 11) Vinayas [SuttaCentral]. Passage-level parallels exist widely across the Sutta Piṭaka and Vinaya, matching discourses such as the *Kakudhatherasutta* (AN 5.100), the *Devadattavipattisutta* (AN 8.7), the *Saṁghabhedasutta* (AN 10.37), and *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Saṅghādisesa* 10 [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus confirms these extensive text reuses, registering major shared passages with the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*—especially AN 5 (matching §2.2.1–2.4.42), AN 10 (§5.2.20–5.3.12), and AN 8 (§4.6.16–4.7.48)—and with *Saṅghādisesa* 10 [DharmaNexus]. Cross-linguistically, DharmaNexus establishes substantial text alignments with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, Tibetan *Vinayavastu* and *Vinayavibhaṅga* sections, and discourses in the Chinese *Ekottarāgama* (T 125) and *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
